implementation_notes: C's language and standard library have no notion of roles or principals, so the split lives in the process model: the two duties run as separate processes under separate user ids, and the only channel between them is a socket or pipe whose messages carry an identity the receiver can verify with the kernel. What replaces the classic role object is that OS boundary plus an explicit credential check: SO_PEERCRED on a connected AF_UNIX stream socket returns the peer's pid/uid/gid as captured at connect()/listen() time, and SO_PASSCRED with SCM_CREDENTIALS attaches sender credentials to each datagram, so the checker daemon can enforce 'the caller approving this request is not the uid that created it' without trusting any field in the payload. In-process role conventions in C are not controls - any code in the same address space can call any function - so where the separation must hold against a compromised component, it has to be a uid, a process or a machine boundary.
pitfalls: In-process role checks in C are advisory: once a request reaches the same address space nothing stops it from performing both halves, so a real separation must be an OS-enforced boundary (different uid, process or machine).

SO_PEERCRED reports the credentials captured at connect()/listen() time and pid alone is not an identity (pid reuse); treat the uid/gid as the stable part and keep the long-lived connection out of the approval path if roles must change.

Trusting a uid or username carried in the message - instead of SO_PEERCRED/SCM_CREDENTIALS - lets the caller assert any identity; when both ends run as the same uid the kernel offers no distinction at all.
